beseech.verb type: action — dynamic; a verb of asking, so it reports a speech act rather than a state. No linking or stative use.
beseech.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is the person begged, and it is obligatory: *the families beseech the governor*, ✗ *the families beseech*. Usually completed by an infinitive (*beseech him to forgive her*) or by *for* + the thing wanted (*besought the judge for one more week*).
beseech.passive: **yes**, though formal like the verb itself — *the judge was besought for one more week*; *the agency has been besought for years to publish the data*.

bring.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, from carrying (*bring your ID*) to causing (*spring brings the tourists back*). No stative or linking use.
bring.transitivity: **transitive**, and freely **ditransitive**: *bring me the file*, *bring her a chair*. The object is obligatory — ✗ *she brought* is incomplete. The particle uses keep the object (*bring up the layoffs*, *bring in a consultant*).
bring.passive: **yes**, and very common — *he was brought up by his grandmother*; *three cases have been brought against the company*; *the resignation was brought about by their reporting*.

buy.verb type: action — dynamic in the purchase, bribery, and *buy out* senses. The *believe* sense (*I don't buy it*) is mental but still takes the progressive: *I'm not buying that story*.
buy.transitivity: **transitive**, and **ditransitive** in *buy her a coffee*, *buy us two more weeks*. The object is normally obligatory (✗ *we bought at the market*), though *buy* can stand alone in shopping contexts: *we buy local*.
buy.passive: **yes** — *the truck was bought used*; *two inspectors were bought off*; *the chain has been bought out by a private equity firm*.

catch.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, including the involuntary ones (*catch a cold*, *catch the joke*). No linking or stative use.
catch.transitivity: **both** — transitive in most senses (*caught the glass*, *caught three fish*), intransitive in *the zipper catches* and in *catch on* / *catch up* (*go ahead; I'll catch up*).
catch.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the driver has been caught*; *two managers have been caught falsifying the logs*. Restricted for the illness sense, where the active is the only natural form: ✗ *a cold was caught by him*.

creep.verb type: action — dynamic, and typically slow or gradual: literal movement (*the cat crept along the fence*) and figurative advance (*costs have crept up*).
creep.transitivity: **intransitive** in every literal and figurative sense — the direction is carried by a preposition (*creep along the rail*, *creep into her emails*). Transitive only in the fixed slang *creep someone out*.
creep.passive: **no** for the movement senses, which have no object at all: ✗ *the fence rail was crept along*. The one passive is the slang idiom — *I was completely creeped out by that mask*.

daydream.verb type: action — dynamic; it names an ongoing mental activity and takes the progressive freely: *he was daydreaming through the lecture*.
daydream.transitivity: **intransitive** — no object at all; what is imagined goes into a prepositional phrase with *about* or *of*: *I daydream about a week with no phone*, ✗ *I daydream a week with no phone*.
daydream.passive: **no** — there is no object to promote: ✗ *a bakery was daydreamed about for years* is not how this is said. Only the awkward prepositional passive is even conceivable, and Americans avoid it.

deal.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses. The *be about* use (*chapter four deals with the war years*) is closer to a state but still takes the ordinary tenses, not the progressive: ✗ *chapter four is dealing with the war years*.
deal.transitivity: **both** — transitive and **ditransitive** in *deal me in*, *deal him four bad hands*, *dealt the plaintiffs a blow*; prepositional-intransitive in *deal with* and *deal in*; bare intransitive in the drug sense (*he got caught dealing*).
deal.passive: **yes** — *the cards were dealt*; *a blow was dealt to the plaintiffs*. The prepositional passive is natural too: *the complaint has already been dealt with*.

dream.verb type: action — dynamic; it names an activity or an experience over time and takes the progressive: *she was dreaming about the house again*. No stative or linking use.
dream.transitivity: **both** — normally intransitive with *about* or *of* (*I dream of a year with no travel*), transitive with a content object (*he has dreamed the same thing three nights running*) and in *dream up a slogan*.
dream.passive: **restricted** — natural only for *dream up*: *the whole plan was dreamed up over one dinner*. The ordinary senses have no passive: ✗ *her grandmother's house was dreamed about*.

feel.verb type: **stative** in the emotion and opinion senses (*I feel better*, *I feel we should wait*) — the opinion sense refuses the progressive: ✗ *I am feeling we should wait*. **Linking (copular)** in *the room feels cold*, *the meeting felt rehearsed*. **Action** only in the deliberate senses: *feel the fabric*, *feel them out*.
feel.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the linking use (*this draft has felt wrong*), transitive in *felt the fabric*, *felt the tremor*, and with a *that*-clause in the opinion sense. *Feel like* takes a noun or an -ing form, never an infinitive: ✗ *feel like to leave*.
feel.passive: **restricted** — fine where the act is deliberate or the sensation is shared: *the swelling was felt and a scan ordered*; *the tremor was felt across three counties*; *the committee has already been felt out*. No passive of the linking use (✗ *cold is felt by the room*) or of the opinion sense (✗ *the price was felt too high by her*).

keep.verb type: action — dynamic, but several senses describe maintaining a state rather than a single act (*keep the shop warm*, *keep asking*). The resultative pattern *keep the door open* is complex-transitive, not linking: the adjective describes the object, not the subject.
keep.transitivity: **both** — transitive in most senses, and complex-transitive with an added adjective, participle, or place (*keep them waiting*, *keep the keys in the drawer*). Intransitive in the freshness sense: *hard cheese keeps for months*. *Keep* + -ing only: *keep trying*, ✗ *keep to try*.
keep.passive: **yes** — *every letter she sent him was kept*; *records have been kept since 1830*; *we were kept awake by the noise*. No passive of the intransitive sense: ✗ *for months is kept by hard cheese*.

kneel.verb type: action — dynamic; it covers both the movement down (*he knelt to tie his son's shoe*) and staying in the position (*she has knelt there for an hour*).
kneel.transitivity: **intransitive** — never takes an object: ✗ *she knelt the floor*. Purpose or place is added by a phrase (*kneel on the stone steps*, *kneel to see the bottom shelf*).
kneel.passive: **no** — an intransitive verb has nothing to promote to subject: ✗ *the stone steps were knelt on by the pilgrims* is at best strained, and the protest sense has no passive at all.

lean.verb type: action — dynamic in the body senses (*he leaned over the counter*). Closer to **stative** where it reports a standing tilt or tendency: *the old barn leans two degrees east*, *the county leans Republican*.
lean.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in most senses (*don't lean out that far*, *I leaned toward the cheaper option*), transitive when you prop something: *she had leaned her bike against the wrong tree*.
lean.passive: **restricted** — possible only in the propping sense: *the ladder was leaned against the wall*. No passive of the tendency or posture senses (✗ *toward the cheaper option was leaned*), though the prepositional passive works for pressure: *he was leaned on to sell*.

leap.verb type: action — dynamic, and always a sudden move rather than a gradual one, literally (*deer leap that fence*) or of numbers (*the stock leapt again*).
leap.transitivity: **intransitive** — the destination or obstacle comes with a preposition (*leapt from the counter*, *leaped at the chance*). What looks like an object in *leap that fence* is a path phrase, not a true object.
leap.passive: **no** — there is no object to promote: ✗ *the chance was leaped at by her* is not idiomatic, and ✗ *conclusions are leapt to* survives only as a set phrase.

leave.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, from departing (*we leave at six*) to bequeathing (*her aunt left her the cabin*). The resultative *leave the door open* is complex-transitive, not linking.
leave.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in *they left before the second act*, transitive in *don't leave your laptop in the car*, and **ditransitive** in *left her the cabin*, *I have left you three voicemails*.
leave.passive: **yes**, and constant — *two blocks have been left without power*; *two names were left out of the credits*; *nothing was left of the barn but the foundation*. Note that *left* in *two cookies left* is an adjective, not a passive.

lose.verb type: action — dynamic, though most senses report a change of state the subject did not choose (*he lost his job*, *she lost her father*). *Lost* in *I am lost* is an adjective, not a tense.
lose.transitivity: **both** — transitive in nearly every sense (*lost her keys*, *lost his temper*), intransitive in the competition sense: *that team loses whenever it rains*.
lose.passive: **yes** — *the game was lost in overtime*; *the receipt had been lost*; *two months have been lost to review*. The bereavement sense resists it: ✗ *her father was lost by her* is not how this is said.

may.verb type: **modal auxiliary** — never a main verb. It has no -s form (✗ *he mays*), no -ing form (✗ *maying*), and no participle (✗ *I have might*); *might* is its past, used for backshift (*she said we might need a second interview*) and as a weaker present possibility.
may.transitivity: Neither — a modal takes no object. It is followed by a bare infinitive, never by *to*: *you may leave*, ✗ *you may to leave*. Past possibility uses *may have* / *might have* plus a participle.
may.passive: **no** — a modal has no passive of its own: ✗ *permission was mayed*. It combines freely with a passive infinitive, which is a different thing: *the form may be signed once it is witnessed*.

mean.verb type: **stative** in the core senses — signify (*that symbol means the same thing*), entail (*a second round means another two weeks*), and matter (*your opinion means more to him*). All refuse the progressive: ✗ *that symbol is meaning*. **Action** only in the intention sense: *I meant to call you back*.
mean.transitivity: **transitive** — the object may be a noun (*meant nothing to her*), a *that*-clause (*what I mean is that we can't ship*), or an infinitive (*I don't mean to interrupt*). The object is obligatory: ✗ *the red light meant* is incomplete.
mean.passive: **no** in the stative senses — this is one learners get wrong: ✗ *the same thing is meant by that symbol*, ✗ *a great deal has been meant to my family by that*. The only passive is the fixed *be meant for* / *be meant to* (*you are meant to sign both copies*, *they were meant for each other*), which has no matching active.

outthink.verb type: action — dynamic, inflecting exactly like its base *think*, but only in the competitive sense: to beat someone mentally. No stative or linking use.
outthink.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — ✗ *their defense outthought* is incomplete. The object is a person or a side, or a reflexive in the self-defeating sense: *he outthought himself*.
outthink.passive: **yes** — *our defense was outthought for four quarters*; *every negotiator they have sent has been outthought*. The reflexive use has no passive, as expected.

oversleep.verb type: action — dynamic, and always accidental, which is what separates it from the deliberate *sleep in*.
oversleep.transitivity: **intransitive** — takes no object at all: *if I oversleep, start without me*, ✗ *I overslept my alarm*. What was missed goes in a separate clause: *he overslept and missed his connection*.
oversleep.passive: **no** — an objectless intransitive has no passive: ✗ *the alarm was overslept*.

rethink.verb type: action — dynamic; a prefixed *think* used only in the deliberate sense of reconsidering, so it lacks *think*'s stative opinion use.
rethink.transitivity: **transitive** in normal use — *we should rethink the launch date*, *rethought the whole budget*. The object can be left out when it is obvious from context (*the board may have to rethink*), but it is usually present.
rethink.passive: **yes** — *the whole budget was rethought in one afternoon*; *the return policy has been rethought twice this year*.

seek.verb type: action — dynamic, and formal in American English, where speech prefers *look for*. No stative or linking use.
seek.transitivity: **transitive** — the object is what you want (*sought damages*, *seeks comment*), and it is obligatory: ✗ *rescuers sought for three days* needs *the hikers*. It also takes an infinitive: *the bill seeks to close that loophole*.
seek.passive: **yes**, and idiomatic in official prose — *damages were sought in federal court*; *comment has been sought from both sides*. The participle has also hardened into an adjective: *the most sought-after editor in town*.

sleep.verb type: action — dynamic; it names an ongoing activity and takes the progressive freely (*the baby is sleeping*). The capacity sense (*the cabin sleeps six*) is **stative** and resists it: ✗ *the cabin is sleeping six*.
sleep.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the ordinary sense, with no object: *I slept badly*, ✗ *I slept a bad night*. Transitive only in the capacity sense, where the object is a number of people: *the cabin sleeps six*.
sleep.passive: **no** — ✗ *six are slept by the cabin*, and the ordinary sense has no object at all. The particle verbs do passivize: *the offer was slept on and countered Monday*; *the jet lag was slept off on the couch*.

sweep.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, literal (*sweep the porch*) and figurative (*the fire swept through the canyon*, *their film swept the technical categories*).
sweep.transitivity: **both** — transitive in *swept the broken glass into a dustpan*, *swept the series*, *swept the room for bugs*; intransitive with a path phrase in the movement senses: *she sweeps into a room*, *a cold front sweeps down the valley*.
sweep.passive: **yes** in the transitive senses — *the room was swept for bugs*; *the complaint got swept under the rug*; *the shop floor has not been swept in a week*. No passive of the movement sense: ✗ *the canyon was swept through by the fire*.

teach.verb type: action — dynamic; the subject can be a person or an experience (*that experience has taught me to read the contract first*). No stative or linking use.
teach.transitivity: **ditransitive**, and also **both** — two objects in *she taught me algebra*, one in *she taught fourth grade*, none at all in *I teach*. English splits the roles Russian *учить* covers: the teacher teaches, the student learns, so ✗ *she learned me algebra*.
teach.passive: **yes**, and either object can become the subject — *I was taught algebra in one weekend*; *algebra is taught in the fall*; *the department has been taught to file on time*.

think.verb type: **stative** in the belief sense (*I think we should wait*), where the progressive is out: ✗ *I am thinking he's wrong*. **Action** in the reasoning sense, where it is normal: *let me think*, *I was thinking of leaving early*.
think.transitivity: **both** — intransitive in the reasoning sense (*he thought for a long moment*), transitive with a *that*-clause (*I think we should wait*) or a concrete object (*think it over*, *thought up three names*), and prepositional in *think about* / *think of*.
think.passive: **restricted** — natural with a concrete object: *this has been thought through more carefully than we did it*; *three names were thought up and all rejected*. The belief sense passivizes only impersonally (*it is thought that the two are related*) — never personally: ✗ *the meeting was thought on Thursday by her*.

upsweep.verb type: action — dynamic, but rare as a finite verb; you meet it mainly as the participle *upswept* used as an adjective (*upswept hair*, *upswept wingtips*).
upsweep.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory — *the stylist can upsweep your hair*, *the designers have upswept the tail fins*. It never means cleaning a room: Americans say *sweep up*, ✗ *upsweep the kitchen*.
upsweep.passive: **yes** — *the tail fins have been upswept on the new model*; *her hair was upswept and pinned*. In practice the same participle is far more often a plain adjective than a real passive.

weep.verb type: action — dynamic, and literary in American English, where ordinary speech says *cry*. The leaking sense (*the old radiator weeps*) is equally dynamic.
weep.transitivity: **intransitive** in every sense — no object: ✗ *she wept the letter*. What is mourned takes *for* or *over*: *nobody is going to weep for a bank*; *historians have wept over the loss of that archive*.
weep.passive: **no** — nothing to promote: ✗ *the letter was wept by her*. The prepositional passive exists but is literary and rare: *a loss much wept over*.

wreak.verb type: action — dynamic, and in modern American English almost frozen inside *wreak havoc*. Note that the past is *wreaked*, not ✗ *wrought*, which historically belongs to *work*.
wreak.transitivity: **transitive**, object obligatory and nearly fixed — *havoc*, *damage*, *vengeance*, *revenge*: *a late frost can wreak havoc on the orchards*, ✗ *a late frost can wreak*. The target follows with *on* or *upon*.
wreak.passive: **restricted** — *havoc was wreaked along sixty miles of coast* is grammatical but stiff; the idiom strongly prefers the active. *Vengeance was wreaked upon the city* survives only in the literary register.
